Both the vicar of  the parish. Padre Renato da Cunha CWALGANTI, and the president  of the local syndicate of rural laborers, Manuel Alves de ARAUJO  Pilho, mphasizod the difficulties encountered by the rural  union which, before the revolution, had to fight on two fronts—  against the Ligas and against the majority of the landowners,  l^e main problem now facing the union, which presently enjoys  a monopoly situation, is its lack of trained leaders, facilities  and equipment, A suggestion is made that assistance, preferably  not tlrirough United States Ooverraaont agencies, be rendered to  unigns such as the Sindioato dos Trabalhadores Rurais de Santo  Antao.  SETTING  One of the centers of rural agitation in the Northeast,  the munlcipio of Vitoria de Santo Antao, had a population of  89,000 in 1900, It is typical of the humid zone (zona da mata)  in that its economy revolves around the growing a net processing  of sugar cane. Conflict followed attempts three local police and several  farm foremen and workers to investigate invasion farm by over two  hundred rural workers reportedly connected with Ligas Camponezaa.  Local leader Miri Liga, Antonio Galdino» among those reported killed.  Six members of group eight which investigating invasion were killed  and other two seriously injured in what practically amounted  massacre at hands large band invaders.  Governor Pedro Gondim has sent strong police reinforcements  into area and has cancelled plans attend housing conference in Chile.  Situation appears under control but exceedingly tense.  Consular Officer Kilday left this morning for Joao Pessoa to  get first hand account situation, particularly since ConGen receiving  increasing rumors possible large scale agitation among Paraiba rural  workers with leadership emanating from Pernambuco. Press reports  Juliao held meetings last Sunday in Sape near scene yesterday's  conflict. (See Enclosure l)  The first and iimst general comment that one can make concerning  this evidence is that increases in Industrial power consiuaption have been  due principally to the establishment of new industries (or new uses as  in case of irrigation by the Usina Bulhoes) rather than to increases in  consumption by established industries. Indeed, the overall increase in  power consumption registered in I965 is almost exactly equal to that of  COPERBO (synthetic rubber) plus Brahma (beer) - two new plants pioneering  the production of new products. In 196k, the small drop in consumption  by industries previously hooked-up to the CHESF system was more than  compensated by the entry into the market of the Ciau Agro Industrial  Igarassu, a manufactirrer of caustic soda belonging to the Josi Ermirio  de Morais (Votorantiaa) group.  The second general coiament that one can make is the apparent non- synchronous occurrence of the recession in the sugar and textile indus­ tries. A small decline in power consumption is registered in I963 by  the listed sugar mills, coinciding with the period referred to locally  as the "time of Arraes" when the activity of the industry was interarupted  frequently by strikes, but recovered subsequently, in all but one case  to levels significantly higher than in I962. On the other hand, consump­ tion by textile miUs continued to increase in I963, dropping in one case  in 1964, but only registering a marked decline in I965 when the indxistry  was seriously affected by the recession of the first semester of the year. [CLS]Forwarding Helping Items of Information[SEP] DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE  THE NATIONAL WAR COLLEGE  WASHINGTON, D.C. 20315  21 January 1966  Dear Mr. Okun:  The National War College has received a telegram designating  you as the Control Officer for the planned visit to Brasilia during  March 1966, and I am writing at this time in order to forward some  items of information that 1 hope will prove helpful to you.  Inclosed are copies of the roster of participants in the field trip, a planning memorandum covering in some detail the guidelines that we have found helpful to project officers during past trips, a suggested press release (.ior use only if deemed advisable!, and a copy of the  effective Non-Attribution Policy. When completed a refined itinerary, a billeting list, aircraft crew list and passport roster will also be forwarded to you.  Present planning provides for the use of a MATS C-135 aircraft, departing Caracas at 0800 Thursday, 17 March, arriving Brasilia about 1350 (Z-3 zone)."- ' (Please confirm zone time. ) Departure for e Rio is scheduled for 0800 Friday, 18 March. Should a C-130 type rtT_ aircraft be substituted for the C-135, there will, of necessity, be  some adjustments in the arrival and departure times. We will con­ firm the itinerary at the earliest possible date.  In reviewing the report of last year's visit to Brasilia, I find  that the participants were enthusiastic about the program and the  arrangements for the conduct of the visit. It appears that a similar  program would fit our needs admirably. Also inclosed is a copy of  a letter sent to Mr. Philip Raine by our Deputy Commandant for  Foreign Affairs, which discusses the subject of the planned visit to  Brasilia and Rio.  Last year's group found the Hotel Nacional to be "Excellent, "  and I would hope that it might again be available to us. It appears  that we would keep the maximum number of people happy if you can  arrange for 14 doubles and 7 singles. Additional doubles can be  utilized if fewer singles are available and this is understood by the  members of the Class. I will send a billeting roster as soon as I  can pin each individual down on preferred roommates etc. [SEP]Defense Affairs 1966 National War College Visit[CLS]

[CLS]Letter to Kenneth D. Frederick re: agricultural development in the Northeast[SEP] January 12th, 1971.  Dr. Kenneth D. Frederick  Division of the Humanities  and Social Sciences  California Institute of Technology  Pasadena, California 91109  Dear Ken:  Many thanks for sending me a copy of your report on agricultural  development in the Northeast. Your study will be particularly valuable  inasmuch as it looks like I will be transferred to Recife around the end  of this month.  I have been through your report very quickly; I want to study  it more carefully in the caning weeks. My first impression is that it is  excellent. I&rticularly, I am pleased to see some analysis on the relative  costs and returns of production of basic crops. It appears you may have  sufficient data for programming; I would encourage you do so, if possible,  especially for small farms. In view of your recommendations on sugar  subsidies and quotas, I would have liked to have seen a little more back­ ground and analysis on these topics. Also, I have some reservations about  the land tax accomplishing significant changes in land use patterns. The  experience in Latin America is that this tax is simply too complex to  manage; even if it were manageable strong vested interests would not allow  it to be enforced. I may wish to modify all these comments, however, after  a second reading.  We are delighted to have your report and feel that it will be  useful and meaningful in the development of our agriculture program in  the Northeast. I was convinced following our quick meeting here last  summer, that we share the same biases about the Northeast. It is good to  see these biases evaluated and substantiated.  Sincerely,  L.Harlan Davis  Deputy Chief, Planning  & Development, ARDO  LHD:icc [SEP]AGR NE AGRICULTURAL PROGRAM General Correspondence[CLS]

MCCARTHY  UPI Latin American Editor  A massive land swindle has been unearthed in Brazil with hundreds of Americans from the Midwest, Southwest and West the victims of unscrup­ulous salesmen to the tune of millions of dollars.  Complaints from American citizens in Texas, Indiana and Utah, among other states, are pouring in to the U.S. Embassy in Rio de Janeiro and the federal gov­ernment in Brasilia.  THEY RANGE from charges of fraud and irregu­larities in registrations and transfers to outright absence of any title to lands bought.  UPI correspondent John Wilson in Rio reports the scandal has reached such proportions the government has ordered a military inquiry and the American Embassy officially urged "caution and prudence" in the further purchase of lands in the Brazilian interior.  AN OFFICIAL letter now being distributed by the embassy to prospective pur­chasers reads "it is most advisable that prospective buyers not commit them­selves without first coming to Brazil for a personal inspec­tion of the land in question," Wilson says.  The embassy also recom mends prospective purchaser discuss taxes, titles and other details with a reputable Bra zilian attorney since the embassy is not authorized to conduct such inquiries,  BRAZILIAN Justice Minis ter Luiz Gamae Silva said this week the background of all persons engaged in selling land in the interior to Americans is being carefull studied and the guilty face legal punishment and expul sion from the country. "We already have evidence on many infractions of our law," he said. An aide. Detective Inspector Newton Quirino said "the swindle runs into the millions of dollars . . . fabulous profits have been made." [SEP]POL32-1 Territory&BoundaryDisputes[CLS]

[CLS]Comments on CASP[SEP] UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE  FOREIGN AGRICULTURAL SERVICE  OFFICE OF AGRICULTURAL ATTACHE  American Embassy  Rio de Janeiro  Our only comment on the present version of CASP is with regard  to the statement on mechanization on page 21.  There seems to be some feeling in the Brazilian Government  that agricultural mechanization should not be encouraged.  This thinking is based on the concept that mechanization will  speed up the exodus of underemployed laborers from farms to  the cities. The idea seems to be that the social cost of this  underemployed labor should be borne by those who have invested  their money in farming.  This concept is similar to that which was the basis for the  pre-revolutionary policy of holding farm prices low to provide  cheap food for city workers. Both policies have the effect of  making farming uneconomical by shifting social costs to the  agricultural sector. Both policies are designed by city  raised economists who have had no practical farming experience.  (This incidentally is one of the results of Brazil's poor  rural education. Rural schools are either non-existent or are  so poor that hardly any rural child can expect ever to arrive  at a policy making position in the Government.) Those who  must earn their living by farming tell us that mechanization  is necessary.  The comparison with India and Pakistan is hardly valid for  Brazil. Those countries are not yet self-sufficient in food  production while Brazil exports a very large proportion of its  agricultural production. Brazil may be more nearly in a class  with the U.S. where farming is no longer a way of life but a  business requiring very large amounts of capital. If Brazil's  agricultural products are to compete in world export markets,  they must be produced at a low unit cost. Even with Brazil's  low wage rates, rural labor cannot compete with machines.  Farming in the Southern U.S. was mechanized when rural labor  was $2.00/day. March 5, 1969  MEMORANDUM TO: Richard Palmer - ADDP  FROM:  SUBJECT: [SEP]AGR NE Palmer's Aborted[CLS]

INTRODUCTION  This report is to alert AID missions and interested AJDD/W personnel to  the substantial expertise on land tenure problems available at the University  of Wisconsin. The Land Tenure Center has been operating since I962 with  support from the University of Wisconsin, U.S. foundations, AID/W and country  programs abroad.  Research is focussed on rural institutions as they affect agricultural  productivity, employment opportunities, income distribution, and resource  allocation. The Center has carried out numerous studies in developing  countries in order to evaluate tenure systems, make recommendations for  legislative changes, suggest more effective land titling procedures, and  devise new patterns of land settlement and use. Alternative methods of  land distribution such as colonization, settlement, governmental transfers,  tax incentives, and other policies hav^extensively studied in Latin  America in connection with Alliance for Progress programs. Development  program impact on migration and employment as well as linkages betweeen  agriculture and urban services, markets, and investment policies are  integral to the overall research approach. Okun, Counselor of Embassy, Brasilia  1. Following are the main conversational points touched on at lunch.  2. New Constitution. PACHECO was pleased with the new constitution which  he thinks will provide an adequate tool for Brazil's future development,  and for the incoming COSTA E SILVA administration. At the same time, he  noted that the constitution had errors and omissions in it. He pointed  out that the Vice President's role as currently provided for in the draft  constitution is a hazy one, and that the constitution as drafted calls for  the President of the Senate to convene joint sessions of "the Congress,"  rather than the President of the Congress who is the Vice.President. [CLS]Terms of Reference of Special Study of Agrarian Problems in Brazil[SEP] OPTIONAL FORM NO. 19  MAY 1962 EDITION  SSA FFMR (41 CFR) 101-11.9  UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT  Memorandum LIMITED OFFICIAL USE  TO : Brian Zipp  FROM : POL: David E. Simcox DATE: June 18, 1976  SUBJECT: Terms of Reference of Special Study of Agrarian problems in Brazil  During your period of assignment to the Political Section, I would  appreciate it if you would do a study, suitable to be used as a report,  of the current extent and nature of agrarian unrest in Brazil.  I request this study in the light of the assumptions, based on frequent  but not detailed comments of our^Braz^ian,^sources, that land invasions  and other forms of agrarian unres€/par£"icuiarly severe in recent years,  most notably in frontier states such as those of the Amazon region,  Mato Grosso and Goias.  Your study should address itself to the following questions:  A) What is the extent, nature, and underlying causes of land problems  in Brazil? To what extent have government policies such as opening  roads to new virgin areas or economic pressures on farmers encouraged  migrations into those areas.  B) What are the forces behind the agrarian movement: are the landless  peasants organized or directed? What is their political strength? Are  there more powerful forces behind the landless peasants, such as large  agricultural interests or corporations, as some suggest now?  C) What are the principal resources and attitudes of the government  in dealing with the problem and how effective has the government been?  Is legislation concerning agrarian problems inadequate or conflicting?  Is the court system inadequate to adjudicate a large number of conflicting  claims? What are the basic problem areas in the land tenure systems  contributing to conflict? How serious is agrarian unrest as a public  order problem, and is the government equipped to deal with it?  D) How is the government dealing with the problem in social and economic  terms, such as by land reform? What is effectiveness of the government's  land reform programs, particularly the performance of such agencies  as INCRA, SUDAM, and the Ministry of Agriculture?  E) Finally, some assessment is necessary as to the overall effect of  agrarian unrest on the political stability and public order climate of  the country and the present government. To relate this to U. S. interests  you should bring in some consideration of how the agrarian problem has  or will impact on the interests of American investors and the general  investment climate. Os brancos tomaram dois tergos dos 25 mil hectares de terra que lhes foram doados pelo Im-perio, empurrando-os gra-dativamente para um terri­torio cada vez menor. Ele comentou nao saber quem tinha mais poder na regiao, se a Funai ou os grupos economicos.  HI [SEP]SOC 14-1 Indians 1976[CLS]

Historically inflation has depreciated Brazilian currency in  circulation and necessitated periodic readjustments of the standard  unit and issuance of new money. Despite various attempts to manufacture  banknotes and coins in Brazil, foreign companies traditionally have  supplied the country's currency needs. The Revolutionary Government in  1965 initiated reform of the nation's monetary system which led to the  reintroduction of coinage in August 1968. Anibal Teixeira - MDB from Belo Horizonte. Born 1933 and active in  politics ever since high school when he was President of the UniSo  Brasileira dos Estudantes Secundarios - UBES (Brazilian Union of Secon­ dary Students). During President Kubitschek's regime, he was Director of  the National Institute of Imigration and Colonization. When now Foreign  Minister MagalhSes Pinto was Governor of Minas Gerais, Teixeira was  Secretary for Supply - a secretariat since abolished by Israel Pinheiro.  Formerly the leader of the Popular Representation Party - PRP, he had  since joined the ranks of the MDB. As a deputy, he participated in a  special commission on social problems, mining and metalurgy traveling to  Europe and Africa. He is a graduate of the National Law School of the  University of Brazil. He is also the author of several publications:  Ideology and Economy, (in which he foresaw the Sino-Soviet split), Elites  and Masses and Immigration and Development as well as some anti-communist  monographs and a monograph titled "The Truth about J.K.". As an obvious  leader with real political potential, Teixeira was recommended for a  leader grant in 1966 and traveled to the States as a leader in June of  1967. He was always cordial with Americans and was reportedly favorably  impressed by his introduction to the U.S. He enjoyed considerable esteem  locally as evidenced by the fact that he was the most voted member of the  MDB block in the last election. On March 8,1968, at approximately 2100 hours a shot from a small -—I  calibre weapon, presumably a pistol, was fired at or in the general direct­ ion of the Consular Residence. The impact point of the bullet was not lo­ cated. A suspect was detained attempting to flee the neighborhood on foot  but later released for lack of evidence, especially the absence of a  weapon in his possession. A squad of police searched vacant lots and other  likely hiding places without locating a weapon.  2* At the time the shot was fired a cocktail party was in progress at the  Residence in honor of Mr. and Mrs. Stanford C. Smith, USATD Public Safety  Advisor. The party was attended by several high police officials, and it  was they who identified the explosion as a shot and took immediate action.  The party had not been publicized outside police and Consulate circles.  Comment;  3. The incident, insignificant in itself, is interesting in view of the  history of bombings at the Consular Residence. The Residence has been  bombed twice and there was a third unsuccessful attempt in the years  196L-66. The bombing incidents always took place in the February-March  period of the years in question. There was no incident in the February- March period of 1967, which happened to coincide with a change of Prin­ cipal Officers, nor have there been any incidents or threats since with  the exception of crank phone calls and letters. Government and the Government of Brazil established diplomatic relations..  According to Deputy Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Shaikh  Muhammad Ibrahim Mas'ud, the initiative came from Brazil, which  proposed appointing resident ambassadors in Jidda and Rio de Janeiro.  The Saudis indicated their readiness to receive a Brazilian ambassador  but declined to open a resident mission in Rio de Janeiro, pleading  budgetary limitations. Mas'ud indicated to Ambassador Eilts that he  considers it unlikely that resident diplomatic missions will be  established in either capital in the near future. The Saudi Ambassador  to Venezuela is expected to be accredited concurrently to Brazil. There  has as yet been no indication which Brazilian Ambassador in the area  may be accredited to Saudi Arabia.  Mas'ud expressed his belief that the motivation behind the Brazilian  initiative was essentially economic and noted particularly Brazilian  interest in selling coffee in Saudi Arabia. The Brazilians in their  approach to the Saudi Government also stressed the sizeable Arab  population in Brazil. On its part, Saudi Arabia appreciates the  Brazilian stance in the United Nations and other forums on political  issues of interest to the Arabs and is also aware of the potential  cultural ties between the two countries resulting from Brazil's Arab  population. In addition, the Saudis recognize Brazil as a potential  market for Saudi oil, although Mas'ud expects little expansion of  trade relations in the immediate future. He observed, for instance,  that there is at present no direct shipping connection between the  two countries. Student Demonstration  A number of incidents over the last two weeks, including the  closing of two Diretorios Academicos and the arrests of numerous  students, and culminating in a clasn between student demonstrators  and police on September 15 in Rio, have heightened tension con­ siderably in the student world.  The September 15 anti-GOB demonstration which, among other things,  protested the imposition of (minimal) tuition changes, was for­ bidden by security authorities. However, using tactics of diver­ sion and dispersion in rush hour traffic which proved successful  in the March 24 demonstration, university and secondary school  students in numbers varyingly estimated from one to four thousand  managed to cause considerable turmoil on the city^ principal  downtown streets for several hours.  Security forces reportedly numbering 10,000 men had been mobilized  and placed under strict orders to avoid violence. Nevertheless,  several tear gas bombs were used and a number of students roughed  up (no serious injuries reported). Over 100 demonstrators were  reportedly arrested, but all except five (who the police said  were not students) had been released by the following morning.  (LIMITED OFFICIAL USE)  COMMENT: Through skillful planning, the radical leftist organizers  of the demonstration seem to have accomplished most of their  objectives. They have shown that they can mount an effective  demonstration notwithstanding official prohibition, aid managed to  provoke enough violence to provide them with evidence of "repress­ ion of students by the government" for use as an issue in the future  and to supply grist for the opposition press mill. Sympathy demon­ strations in Rio and other Brazilian cities are now anticipated.  (CONFIDENTIAL)  2. President Adamant on Disfranchising Power  Statements by various spokesmen during the week have made clear  that President Castello Branco does not intend to relinquish his  power to unseat and disfranchise members of Congress in connection  with the legislative handling of the new constitution. Atmosphere of Optimism  An atmosphere of optimism appears to pervade the  major cities of Brazil today. There is still some hang­ over from the nationalistic euphoria which surrounded  Brazil's victory in international soccer competition.  To this has been added a widespread belief that the country  is making significant economic strides. Many Brazilians  are impressed with the nation's healthy rate of growth  and the material signs of progress on all sides. A  surprisingly broad group of urban Brazilians are par­ ticipating in the stock market boom and are talking al­ most as much about their personal gains in the Rio and  Sao Paulo markets as about soccer games. Supporters of  the government are interpreting the record breaking bull  market as a reflection not only of confidence in the  country's economy but also of tacit approval of the  government's political stance. Few people seem even to  consider the effect which a correction in the largely  speculative market could have.  The optimism regarding the future was given a boost  by the aura surrounding the inauguration of the 22 new  State governors on March 15, and by the celebration  activities on the 7th Anniversary of the Revolution on  March 31. The President states that democracy cannot be maintained in its traditional  or classical form. Democracy is not an end in itself but rather a process  or path by which a determined goal can be reached; it is a formula which  must evolve as society changes. Sparkman  United States Senate  Washington, D. C. 20510  Dear Senator Sparkman:  The Secretary has asked me to reply to your letter of  June 3, 1970, requesting comment on a letter of  Mr. Thomas B. Its population of 1,254,000 (1965 est.) accounts for only 1.5%  of the national figure. Natal, the state capital, ranks 12th  among Brazilian cities and has an estimated population of 200,000.  As is the case with most Brazilian states, Rio Grande do Norte's  population is both essentially rural and unusually young.  Approximately 60% live in rural areas and 69.8% of the popula­ tion is under 30 years of age.  Rio Grande do Norte was first settled in 1598 when expfe- ditions from fernambuco were sent North to control the illegal  trade in Brazil wood. The troops built the Forte dos Reis  Magos on the beach at Natal (the fort is still standing) and  the state generally starts its history from that date. The  Indians then living in the area were the Fotiguares and today  natives of Rio Grande do Norte are still called "Potiguares"  and Natal is the "Capital Potiguar".  A serious communist uprising occurred in Natal in 1935 and  communists supporters briefly controlled the city before being  suppressed by the government. During -vorld Nar II, Natal was  the site of a major 0. S. air base which served as a staging  area for allied attacks on Nazi forces in Africa. The city  became known as the Trampoliin da Vitoria at that time, a fact  older residents of the city are fond of telling American visitors.  President Roosevelt met briefly in Natal in 1944 with Brazilian  President Getulio Vargas and the event is portrayed in a large  painting now hanging in the Governor's Palace. Of all the  cities in the Northeast, Natal is undoubtedly the most pro- American.  END UNCLASSIFIED [SEP]POL 18 Provincial,Municipal & State Government 1967[CLS]

Step U: Formal Request  The Chief-of-Party will be notified by the Project Supervisor  concerning ARDO initial concurrence to proceed with a formal  request. He will then submit to ARDO a formal written request  and justification for the proposed technical services to be  rendered. The letter of request will indicate that the Chief- of-Party has discussed the matter with GOB counterpart  entities concerned.  The request will be accompanied by a written statement of  request from the Rector, Director, or top administrative  officer of the GOB entity for services of the U.S. technician.  The formal request will be routed through the ARDO Project  Supervisor, via the ARDO Program Section to the ARDO Chief.  Step XXI: Final Approval  Approval will be given the request by ARDO Chief if all  required procedures are in order. He will affix his signature  to the statement of request. The signature of the appropriate  Project Supervisor and ARDO program officer will also be  indicated. The Contract Supervisor will then prepare a memo  signed by the ARDO Chief to notify the Chief-of-Party in  writing that the matter has cleared ARDO.  Step IV:  The Chief-of-Party will be responsible for Informing his U.S.  Campus Coordinator that AID/W be requested to initiate formal  Country/Mission clearance. Dear Jack:  We have learned informally of the levels for DO funds for Brazil  being projected for the Congressional Presentation. Unless sub­ sequently changed, these levels are $12.4 million for FY 1969  and $9.5 million for FY 1970; this compares with our request of  $12.98 million for FY I969 and $11.5 million for FY 1970.  With respect to a reduction in FY 1969 to $12.4 million while  our budget projection fear this year was tightly drawn, neverthe­ less, recognizing the appropriation difficulties, we think it Is  not unreasonable and we would be quite prepared to try and live  with it if necessary. We would, however, appreciate your efforts  to keep it from being reduced below that level since further cuts  could create real difficulties.  The figure of $9.5 million for FY 1970 is more surprising and  gives us more concern. The specific purpose of this letter, in  fact, is to call this to your personal attention and ask you to  intercede in getting the figure restored to, if possible, the  $11.5 million level which we projected in the recent CAP. We  realize, as has been suggested, that with the coming change in  administration there may be many changes in store and also op­ portunities to readjust the figures at a later date. We also  realize, however, that once a budget figure is established it  tends to be locked in and the process of changing it later,  particularly upward, is much more difficult, time consuming,  and uncertain than if the figure had been established at the  proper level in the first place.  We are also concerned since the $9.5 million level is only an  "asking" figure. Any further cuts which Congress might make  could result in a final figure well below $9.5 million. Dear Jack:  In several recent Manual Orders (1023.3—April 11, IQ69, and 1331.1—  May 23, I969, for example), we have noted increasing emphasis upon  technical assistance loans as distinct frcm capital loans. There is  also, in connection with E-l instructions, increasing indication  that Washington wants PL and DG funds grouped under common objectives  rather than being treated as completely separate entities.  As we move out of infrastructure, etc. and into Title IX emphasis on  the softer sectors, such as education agriculture, health, and munic­ ipal activities, it is evident that our loans are going to be more  related to or composed of technical assistance components. This  suggests more than ever that the treatment of loans as completely  separate from and unrelated to technical assistance is obsolete and  unrealistic.  One could take the position that is held in acme circles in Washington  and reflected in M.O.'s 1201.1 and 1301.1 that we have activities  rather than loans and grants. Activities are divided into two cate­ gories: capital assistance and technical assistance. Both categories  could be funded with loan and/or grant monies (and presumably local  currency as well).  According to M.O. 1201.1, capital assistance activities are (a) con­ struction over $100,000 including advisory services, (b) a feasibility  study of specific potential capital project or projects, and (c) as­ sistance including advisors to development banks and other inter­ mediate credit institutions. [CLS]February Political Report[SEP] POLITICAL REPORT February 1968  The highlight for the month of February was the trip made by Governor  Danilo Areosa to South Brazil. He was in South Brazil for approxima­ tely two weeks. During this time he talked with Federal authorities  from President Costa e Silva on down. According to reports there were  considerable discussions of the problems of the Amazon, many promises  made, that only time will tell whether they are carried out.  Main topics discussed with the President were the problem of the  rubber plantation owners. Governor Areosa has requested a 40% increase  for rubber extracted in this region. The Zona Franca was discussed at  length. There was a request made by the Governor for the President to  re-examine Law 340 which was passed last December. Law 340 mainly  effects the advantages given to tobacco, cigarrett, and beer factories.  This law singles these types of industries as not being eligible for  the benefits of Zona Franca.  While in Rio Governor Areosa visited the French Ambassador. Charges have been made public here that an American has masterminded a huge land swindle. The Brazilian Government has ordered a thorough investigation with a view to pos­sibly declaring null and void the sale of nearly 200,000 acres in the central and north­western parts of Brazil — principally in the States of Amazonas, Mato Grosso, and Goias — to more than 3,000 Americans. Brazilian authorities charge that Stanley Amos Selig, an American, operating through Selig Brothers Real Estate Company of Indi­anapolis, Indiana, has been selling land, generally in 500-acre lots, to much of which he has no valid title.  Other violations charged  Even if the titles to certain of his lots are  good, their sale in smaller lots to individyals  is said to be illegal, on the grounds that  Mr. Selig failed to obtain permission for  parceling them out and properly registering  the sales with the Brazilian Institute of  Agrarian Reform (IBRA) and the National  Institute of Agrarian Development (INDA),  as required by Brazilian law. Mr. Selig himself left Brazil before the story broke, reportedly owing nearly $70,000 in back taxes, while the government issued a warrant for the arrest of his principal Bra­zilian assistant, Joao Inacio Arruda, who is suspected of having escaped to Venezuela with more than a quarter of a million dol­lars. Two of his other close collaborators, Wilson Dias Rocha, a Brazilian, and Arpad Sznecs, a Hungarian, are in custody to testi­fy in the inquiry.  The police recently raided Mr. Arruda's residence and office in Campinas, near Sao Paulo. DATE SENT  12/1/70  Brazilian Wheat Policy and Outlook  If weather conditions continue to be favorable, Brazil, last month  (October), will have begUn the harvest of a record 1.5 million M. T.  wheat crop. This would compare with an average annual crop from 1960- 1965 of 290 thousand metric tons, or a five-fold increase in five years.  Though policies dating as far back as the 1930's, Brazil has spent a  great deal of money to provide its producers with the incentives and  tools necessary to increase wheat production.  Though average per hectare yields remain at a relatively low level  and the crop is forever threatened by an unstable and unpredictable  climate situation, Brazilian wheat production has expanded dramatically.  Production now meets almost 50% of national consumption requirements.  The above facts raise a key question*: Has Brazil reached a wheat  production plateau or will crop increases still continue to occur at  an accelerated pace ? At the moment, Brazil can look back on several  years of optimal wheat growing climate conditions; however, such weather  is not likely to continue forever. In addition, the planting of new land  to wheat is a finite activity. Thus, great new production increases will  not come from this source either.  This airgram will attempt to review recent wheat production trends and  policies in Brazil. Comments cm I'ur&ue Proposal, Economic  Analysis of Technical Change  This proposal involves economic analysis of various policy issues connected  with alternative technologies in producing corn and grain sorghum. In later  stages, research would include other crops. Issues such as impact on out­ put, employment, and income distribution are mentioned. Research would be  related to Brasil, Argentina, Colombia, and perhaps Pakistan.  The research objectives are worthwhile, and Purdue has the expertise.  However, I recommend that AID/Brazil not support the proposal in its present  form.  1. The proposal is inadequately linked, in its presentation, to the ISIPEA/MA  research program in selected products.  2. The proposal shows no awareness of EAPA/MA.  5. Proposal would contribute inadequately to institution-building in Brazil  and other countries, by evidently being primarily located in the U.S..  4. Proposed staffing at the senior level is highly fragmented: 40$ in one  case, 12-30$ for 5 others for the J years. This includes 20'^ of the time  of Ed Schuh for 6 raonths, and 15$ for 2 years, for all countries.  A budget of $680,000 is proposed, for 3 years, looking toward  as yet unbudgeted. Let us assume l/3 to i/2 of this charged against aid to  Brazil.  I propose that comparable resources would be better used in Brazil on the  same research problem, within quite a different framework. The institutional  linkage should be principally (not incidentally) to EEFEA (the EPE Loan  Program) and EAPA of MA. The analysis should concentrate on "improved" tech­ nologies identified and proposed under the BNPEA research program. The senior  staffing should be concentrated with 2 or 3 people, who would he able to spend  significant time with host institutions. This kind of structure would con­ tribute more to Institution-building objectives, especially to real linkage  between teclinical and economic research. The following paper Is a summary account  of the status of political and religious lib­ erties In Brazil, and Is not Intended to serve  as an In-depth or comprehensive analysis.  Governing through three successive presi­ dents, the Brazilian military have been in  power since a coup d'etat on March 31- Aprll 1, 1964 toppled the leftist-oriented gov­ ernment of Joao Goulart. In their desire to  achieve the Brazilian "economic miracle."  and In Implementing their conservative po­ litical model, the governments of Presidents  Castelo Branco, Costa e Silva, and Garra­ stazu Medici, all from the senior ranks of the  armed forces, have concentrated great power  In the executive branch of government and  have taken strong measures in the name of  national security. Some of these measures,  undertaken In the quest for the stability the  military feel Is necessary to accomplish the  economic and political goals, have led to  •worldwide censure and criticism by promi­ nent organizations that have charged that  the Brazilian governments have been authori­ tative and repressive.  In the first week after the coup, the Gov­ ernment arrested over 7.000 people In order  to secure firm control of the country. During  the Castelo Administration, the "political  party system was reorganized so that only  two parties were permitted to function: the  Government-sponsored National Renovating  Alliance (ARENA) and the legal opposition,  the Brazilian Democratic Movement (MDB).  Decree laws were passed which gave military  courts Jurisdiction over crimes related to na­ tional security and a new constitution em­ powered the President to Issue decree laws  and declare states of siege without prior ap­ proval of Congress. Decree 314 of March 14. 1967,  various violations of the law, such as those  governing the press, were considered political  crimes, as were strikes. *  Opposition protests, which began to devel­ op during the Castelo government, became  more widespread under the Costa e SUva Ad­ ministration and the military countered.  Bloody clashes, which occurred In March- April 1968 between students and soldier* led  to official protests from national church lex­ ers. Various Incidents Including  the killing of a U.S. Army captain In Sao  Paulo, soldier-student clashes. Congress' re­ fusal to void the congressional Immunity of  b severe critic of the military, a Supreme  Court order releasing student leaders ar­ rested for attempting to hold a national con­ vention of the outlawed National Union of  Students, and pressure on Costa e Silva by  hardline military elements to respond to such  challenges to 'their authority,' led to the  promulgation of Institutional Act No. 6,  Which was signed on December 13, 1968.  Under Institutional Act No. 5, Congress  was suspended and many citizens, including  some opposition politicians and three state  governors, were arrested on charges of sub­ version. It Is estimated that In the period  Irora the promulgation of the Act until Octo­ ber 1969, 521 persons lost their political  rights. Included among them were many  Members of Congress and members of state  legislatures; a number of state legislatures  were suspended. In January 1969. three Jus­ tices of the Supreme Court were removed and  the Chief Justice resigned In protest." In Feb­ ruary 1969, the Government banned student  and faculty protests and In April It ordered  the retirement of G8 prominent professors,  many of whom were not politically active  and some of whom were well-known con­ servatives.'  The Costa e Silva Administration con­ tinued to act against dissidents through a  series of decrees and Institutional acts such  as Decree Law 898 of September 1969 which  reintroduced the death penalty for political  crimes." Dr. Otavio Gouveia de Bulhoes outlined several key current financial  issues confronting Brazil in a talk given before the Commercial Association  of Rio. Dr. Bulhoes is a professor of economics at the Getulio Vargas  Foundation and was Minister of Finance under the Gastelo Branco Government.  The reviews expressed by Dr. Bulhoes are significant in that he is one  of the architects of Brazil's post-revolution economic policies and is  regarded as a competent and careful observer of the Brazilian economic  scene. The issues presented to the public by Dr. Bulhoes have been the  subject of much discussion in informed economic circles during the past  several weeks. Dr. Bulhoes emphasis on the fiscal deficit and the need  to reduce Government personnel was endorsed editorially by the influential  "Jornal do Brasil". A brief summary of his main points follows:  a. Inflation Risk Continues: Bulhoes poses the persistent Treasury deficit  as the main problem threatening to renew inflation. Monetary authorities  are confronted with the dual problem of financing the Treasury deficit  and furnishing credit to the private sector to meet growing demand for  both producer and consumer goods. When bank credit recently tightened  the Central Bank came under increasing pressure from the private sector  to make credit easier and at last succumbed to these pressures and took  a series of measures to make more credit available. Tight credit had bad  effects on economic activity; and now liberalization brings undesirable  consequences.  b. The Febrerista, regular Liberal, and Christian Democratic opposition,  which /together form the self-denominated democratic opposition to the  GOP, (Emb A-388, March 17, 1965) issued a strongly worded statement  (copy enclosed) on April 14 appealing to the GOP to "restore democracy"  as the only way to unite the nation in defense of "our sovereignty and  independence" in the face of Brazilian "aggression at Guaird." FILE DESIGNATION  HANDLING INDICATOR  TO LIMITED. .OFFICIAL USS T^rU"*3 ^  fit Department of,State  ' A>t.;;H  FROM : Amembassy RIO DE JANEIRO DATE: January 27, 1971  SUBJECT : The Superior Military Court During 1970  REF  TDuring 1970 the Superior Military Court (STM) considered"1  1,249 cases appealed from lower military courts, according  to a Jornal do Brasil report dated January 24. In 702  of these the defendants were absolved, and in 547 they  were found guilty. These appeal rulings reportedly dealt  with two-thirds of the subversion cases tried in Brazil  during the year, and are a considerably larger number than  the STM had reviewed in previous years. The President of  the STM had earlier told the Army Attache of his deliberate  effort to increase the scope of judicial review of the  STM so as to bring increased order into the military  justice area, which the Court felt to be too disorganized.  With reference to habeas corpus petitions considered  during 1970 by the Superior Military Court 154 applications  were made to it, of which only 25 were approved. This  high rate of refusal to grant habeas corpus was attributed  to the existence of Institutional Act No. 5, which denies  habeas corpus in cases of political crimes against national  security. A large number of the cases the Court reviewed  fell into this category.  Some of the more significant cases reviewed by the STM  during the year concerned alleged violations of national  security by writers and editors. Caio Prado Junior had  his lower court sentence of 4 years reduced to 1-1/2 years  by the STM (see Rio's A-17). PASS SALVADOR-;< SAO PAULO  Sep 15 5 oo PH 7Z  FROM : Amconsul BELEM ANALYSIS BRANCHIATE:  SUBJECT : Changeover in Leadership of Regional Development Agencies  REF  r  7T SUMMARY  In early August the heads of SUDAM, SUFRAMA and SUDECO  announced their resignations. Their replacements were  immediately named. Although the incumbents of the  positions have held them for congiderable periods of  time, their replacement is more than a change in.  personnel. The Ministry of Interior seems to want  more tough minded or technically knowledgeable leader­ ship in order to get better results from the fiscal  incentive money channels through those agencies.  On August 8, General Ernesto Bandeira Coelho, director of SUDAM  (Superintendency for the Development of the Amazon Region), announced  that he was going to resign as of August 21, 1972. The resignation  of his executive secretary, Manoel Reis, was announced at the same  time. The following day Cel. Floriano Pacheco, director of SUFRAMA  (Superintendency of the Free Zone of Manaus), also announced his  resignation. The director of SUDECO (The Superintendency for the  Development of the Central West Region) announced his resignation at  the same time. Since that agency's area of responsibility falls out­ side the reporting officer's consular district, comments in this air- gram are limited to SUDAM and SUFRAMA. Cel. Milton Camara Sena was  immediately named to replace Bandeira and Hugo de Almeida was promptly  named to replace Pacheco. It was his impression that Brazil had entered a phase of its political evolution  whose importance could not be ignored by the U. S. Government. Following two  years of instability and efforts to find the right road that marked the parlia­ mentary experiment, the present Government was in a position of firm authority  derived from the will of the people as expressed in the recent plebiscite*  That Government was now ready to carry out a financial policy that would have  significant political consequences. If that  policy were successful in attaining those goals, then Brazil could consolidate  its position as one of the truly important democracies in the Western World.  Brazil was fully aware of the fact that on today's world stage there was something  else in addition to the U.S.-Soviet conflict. That was an emerging European force  wanting to be independent and to attract into its sphere of influence the new  African nations. What there was was a concerted and integrated effort to  create a neo-capitalism unlike anything that ever existed before in Brazil. That ^  fact was more important than any isolated pronouncement by this or that political  leader. The situation in Brazil had to be viewed as a de facto situation and  all its consequences realistically gauged.
